name: Fractured Margin
description: Fractured Margin is a medium rocky world that appears to have been subjected to forces beyond normal geology. Its surface is split by canyon systems and rift valleys that form a near-perfect grid pattern across the largest continent, as if the crust were scored by an enormous blade before being pulled apart. The canyon walls are unnaturally smooth and vertical, dropping hundreds of meters to floors of pulverized rock. A massive meteor crater at the southern pole is the only feature that follows natural formation patterns.

The thin atmosphere whistles through the grid-pattern canyons, creating a low, persistent harmonic that changes pitch as the wind shifts direction. The magnetic poles are unstable and unpredictable, occasionally flipping orientation within hours rather than millennia, a phenomenon that causes compass-equivalent instruments to spin uselessly. The light is harsh and clear during the day, casting the geometric canyon shadows in sharp relief, while nights are utterly dark and bitingly cold.

An automated distress beacon has been broadcasting from the deepest intersection of the canyon grid for an estimated four hundred years. Three expeditions have attempted to reach it, and all three reported spatial anomalies near the source—distances that did not match measurements, paths that led back to their starting points, and equipment that recorded impossible coordinates. The prevailing theory is that the canyon grid marks the margins of a spatial rift or wormhole event that fractured normal space-time in this location.

Fractured Margin has been classified as a navigational hazard, with the spatial anomalies extending into the near-orbital environment during the magnetic pole reversals. The distress beacon continues to broadcast, its signal degrading slowly but never quite falling silent. Ships that pass too close during active periods report brief sensor ghosts—contacts that appear and vanish in fractions of a second, bearing transponder codes from vessels that have never been registered in any known database. The margin between normal space and whatever lies beneath these fractures remains dangerously thin.
